story: Soli
text: Google finally ships a research project in a real product and people don’t seem to understand the usefulness. Human nature for some reason often devolves to “what’s the point?” Here’s the 2015 announcement. There’s a lot of potential. Maybe we’d all benefit from “imagine what’s now possible “ [VIDEO]

story: Pens Are Making a High-Tech Comeback
text: Better pen input would be great, especially for drawing. How about some form of chorded keyboard or glove? A chorded keyboard was demonstrated in 1968 by Engelbart: [LINK] Google's Soli project might lead to better input: [VIDEO]

text: How long before gestures move off the screen surface? This technology got off to an exciting start but it quickly hit a wall. It was disappointing, for example, when Microsoft had to unbundle the Kinect. Microsoft's Kinect - 2010 Leap Motion - 2010 Intel Real Sense - [LINK] Google's Soli chip - 2016 - [VIDEO] Google's Touch Sensitive Fabric: [LINK]

story: OptiKey – Full computer control and speech with your eyes
text: This tool is for people who can't use their hands, of course. For the average person, we're pretty close to being able to use voice instead of typing. [LINK] [LINK] Throw in eye tracking and precise gestures ( [VIDEO] ) and the keyboard isn't necessary.

story: Using a Custom Keyboard for CSS
text: It would be great if some of the repetitive tasks didn't even require a keyboard but rather use subtle gestures, eye tracking, and voice commands. Leap Motion, for example, never panned out but Google's Soli project might get us there: [VIDEO] Throw in better autocompletion ( [LINK] ) and software development becomes more precise and less repetitive.

story: How Long Will We Keep Typing?
text: No one said that the solution has to be all speech. Throw in some small gestures and that'll be faster than reaching for a key. [VIDEO] Throw in eye-tracking and you can pick out any word quickly.

story: Ultrasound technology lets you touch and manipulate virtual objects
text: Gesture based computing is almost here in some form. Apple, Google, Intel and Microsoft are all working on it: Apple: [LINK] Intel Real Sense - [LINK] Google's Soli chip - [VIDEO] Microsoft shipped the Kinect 6 years ago. The need for hand tracking with VR headsets should give it another boost. By the 20th anniversary of Minority Report? [LINK]

story: An engineer replaced four monitors with Meta glasses
text: "The keyboard is the only thing I need, except for the glasses." I think this loses a lot of appeal until we can throw away the keyboard. We should be able to do better. Hopefully, Google ships this silicon this year: [VIDEO] I'd rather have those monitors and no keyboard.

story: An iPhone Is an Extension of the Mind
text: Paper notebooks might be. [LINK] The cell phone, etc will be a much bigger extension. However, we still need better ways to input, organize and access the information. Handwritten notes, voice memos, pictures, drawings, unstructured and structured data, etc. Cortana/Siri with hand tracking ( [VIDEO] ) and a HoloLens will allow people to organize everything in creative ways.

story: My Journey From Blindness to Building a Fully Conversational User Interface
text: you can provide audible feedback when you move your hands. Many gestures don't provide anyone tactile feedback. Move your hands or fingers then something happens on the screen. Google's new chip could probably help interpret a series of gestures: [VIDEO]

story: FingerIO: Using Active Sonar for Fine-Grained Finger Tracking
text: Really interesting. Reminds me of SOLI (which is radar rather than sonar): [VIDEO] Is there a way of trying this out? I know it'd only be demo line drawing applications but it'd still be interesting to try.

story: Running Emacs on Android
text: Now we need a gesture keyboard so we can type, or twitch, instead of using an onscreen keyboard. Finger IO: [LINK] Google's Soli: [VIDEO] Perhaps a modified game controller: [LINK]

story: SignAloud: Gloves That Translate Sign Language into Text and Speech
text: Someone could devise a more subtle set of movements for text entry. Google's Soli would recognize small movements: [VIDEO] There are others: [LINK]

story: Blind Apple engineer is transforming the tech world at only 22
text: i'm disappointed that we haven't made more progress with voice interfaces. Many people are happy with the keyboard/mouse as their primary input devices but combined with subtle gestures like you might get with Google's Soli and we should get a better user interface for everyone. [VIDEO]

text: How about a little more innovation in keyboards? It is 30 years later. Split keyboards? [LINK] Tenting capable? Add a Soli chip? [VIDEO]

text: Voice, eye tacking, and gesturing don’t offer possibilities? [VIDEO] [LINK] And yes, if you’re clicking away in a room of programmers, it won’t work for you, but with a Hololens I’ll find a quiet location.

story: The future of the human-computer interface?
text: How old are you? It’s really not that hard to imagine the keyboard being replaced by one, or a combination, of technologies in the next decade or two. Voice has gotten dramatically better in the past few years. Another decade? There are also gesture technologies: [VIDEO] Anyway, if you’ve got 3 or 4 decades of life, you still think we won’t have sufficient advances to replace the keyboard?

story: Introducing Oculus Go, Plus Santa Cruz Updates
text: In my dreams the keyboard disappears. My eyes, or fingers, move the cursor, I can speak interactively with the computer, gesture, etc. Can fingers/hands be tracked sufficiently to provide an accurate soft keyboard? [VIDEO]

There's more info here on how it's used: [LINK] EDIT: found the original presentation: [LINK] . I think the touch sensitive cloth project also made it into a few products.

story: Controlling a Quadcopter with Hand Gestures
text: Hand Gesture controls bother me. I see all these fancy implementations enabling hand gestures such as the Google ATAP project called Soli [1], but none of these replace haptical feedback. One of the major aspects of any haptical human-to-machine interface is feedback and robustness. When you turn a high quality 30 indent encoder from Alps [2] or avionics grade Elma encoder [3]; you'll realize the value of haptic feedback. There is a reason why cockpits are full of knobs and dials, although unfortunately, that's changing due to highly integrated multi-function glass instruments. Problem with hand gestures is robustness. Theramins (hand gesture based music instrument) are cool, but they take forever to master and I am not saying they are trying to replace pianos, but let's just say - iPad pianos are not fun precisely because of the lack of feedback. I really think gesture based controls are inferior. They have no place in my living room, my car or anywhere in my life. That said, I think the implementation of hand gesture based systems as pointed out in this article are truly interesting. It is a challenging problem. [1] [VIDEO] [2] [LINK] [3] [LINK]
